text: You get a string made of open parentheses, close parentheses, and stars. Each star can be an open, a close, or an empty string. Return true if some choice makes the string a valid parenthesis string.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — valid means the usual rule. Every open has a matching close after it, and reading left to right, I never close more than I've opened. And each star picks its own role, so two stars can pick different things. Is that right?
Yes. Each star is free to choose.

Okay. One thing I want to say early. With no stars, I'd keep one number: the count of open brackets. With stars, that count can be many values at once. So I want to track the range of possible open counts — l, the fewest I could have, and r, the most. Are there any constraints on the input size?
The string has between one and a hundred characters, and every character is an open, a close, or a star.

Got it. Small input, but a hundred stars still means three to the hundredth choices, so I can't try them all. Quick check on the examples: the plain pair is true; open, star, close is true with the star as empty; and open, star, close, close is true with the star as an open. All three match.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. A naive approach tries all three-to-the-k ways to fill the stars — exponential. A step up is a DP over the set of reachable open counts, which is correct but quadratic. This problem reminds me of the classic balance-counter check for parentheses, plus a greedy idea: instead of trying every choice, I track the range of possible open counts. An open shifts the range up by one, a close shifts it down, and a star widens it by one on each side. The key fact is that the reachable counts are always contiguous — no gaps — so two ints are enough.
How sure are you that two numbers are enough?

I checked it. Against brute force on every string of length one to ten — eighty-eight thousand, five hundred seventy-two strings — zero mismatches. Against the set DP on over two point three million strings of length eleven to thirteen, plus fifty thousand random strings up to length a hundred — zero mismatches again. And l stayed at or below r at every step.

Here's the plan. One: start l and r at zero. Two: an open bumps both, a close drops both, a star drops l and bumps r. Three: if r goes below zero, return false on the spot; clamp l at zero; at the end, return whether l is zero. So there are two ways to fail: r below zero means too many closes even if every star opens, and l above zero at the end means too many opens. One thing worth flagging — the clamp. A negative count is a dead choice, not a real state. Without it, a single star breaks: l sits at minus one, so I'd say false, but the star can be empty. The set DP is easier to trust, but the range is linear time and constant space. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. It's one loop over the string with two ints. Each character shifts or widens the range, then I check r below zero to fail early, then clamp l up to zero. After the loop, I return l equals zero. One thing worth flagging — every small line is load-bearing. I tested wrong versions on all short strings. Dropping the clamp gets over twenty-seven thousand wrong, and a single star is enough to break it. Returning false when l goes negative, instead of clamping, also fails on a single star. And checking r only at the end fails on close-then-star, because the star hides the first close that had nothing to match.

Let's dry-run the code. Open, star, close, close — expected true. The step that matters is the first close: the range drops from zero-to-two to minus-one-to-one. Minus one isn't a real state, so I clamp to zero-to-one. One stays alive because the star could be an open, and that lets the last close work. l ends at zero, so true. A failing one: star, close, open ends with l at one — that last open never closes, so false. Corner cases: a single star is true only thanks to the clamp; close then star fails right away, which is why r is checked inside the loop.

Let me think about complexity here. Time is linear — one pass, constant work per character. Space is constant — just two ints, however many stars there are. The worst case is all stars, where brute force needs three to the hundredth tries, but here the range just widens by one each step. Oh, one more thing — there's a two-pass version too. Left to right, treat stars as opens and fail if closes ever win; right to left, treat stars as closes and fail if opens ever win. The first pass is my r check; the second matches my end check on l.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You turned an exponential number of choices into a range, and explained why it has no gaps, so two ints are enough. You named the two ways to fail: r below zero during the pass, and l above zero at the end. And you showed the clamp is needed for correctness, with a single star as the one-character proof. Plus the two-pass follow-up. Good work.
